Modal Verbs in the Passive Voice

You use modal verbs to add meaning to other verbs. They come before the dictionary form (Infinitive without 'to') of the main verb.
Modal verbs (can, must, have to, may, might) can add meaning connected with certainty or obligation.

You can use modal verbs in the passive voice.
You use the passive voice when you want to focus on the receiver of the action, rather than the 'doer' of the action.

Here is the structure of a passive sentence:

Subject + To be + past participle

For example:
They are threatened by those criminals they can testify against.

You can add a modal verb before the To be.

Subject + modal + To be + past participle

For example:
They may be threatened by those criminals they can testify against.

Here the sentence now has an additional meaning of possibility, thanks to the modal may.
They may be threatened by those criminals they can testify against.
Generally, these individuals should be protected by the police until the trial.
After their release they should be sent to other cities with new identities.
The Present Perfect Continuous Tense vs. Present Perfect Tense

You use the Present Perfect Continuous tense to talk about an action that began in the past and is still continuing to the present time.

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action that has a connection to the present time. The action either finished in the past, just recently finished or, in some cases, continues to the present time.

The main difference between these two tenses is that you use the Present Perfect Continuous when you want to emphasize that the action began in the past and is still continuing now.

Some verbs are NOT used in the continuous form. Some common examples are: to be, to have and to know.

You often use the Present Perfect Continuous with words that talk about a period of time continuing up to the present, like recently, this week, since March, for the last two days.

images.text: What is the Witness Protection Program? It is a program that protects witnesses who are willing to testify against criminals. It has been protecting people since the 1960s. It now includes up to a thousand witnesses every year, at a cost of millions of US dollars.

Some of the protected witnesses are innocent citizens who unintentionally witness a violent crime. They may be threatened by those criminals they can testify against. Generally, these individuals should be protected by the police until the trial. Afterwards, they are supposed to be relocated to another part of the country, or in some cases even to another country.
The Justice Department is supposed to arrange new identities, new homes and new jobs for them.

Often witnesses are convicted criminals who are willing to testify against other criminals. For example, some of them are allowed to keep part of the money they gained illegally. They are supposed to be kept safe until the trial. Many witnesses have been hiding in a protected prison cell or in a secret hiding place such as a mountain hideaway or a hotel room.

After their release they should be sent to other cities with new identities.
From the beginning, there has been much public criticism of the Witness Protection Program. Critics claim that "making deals" with murderers and other violent criminals is bad.
